latest_final: The narrator is a living human whose romantic partner is now dead; the narrator intentionally caused the partner's death—it was no accident—and now faces likely arrest and legal punishment. To cover the killing, the narrator fabricated a note instead of keeping any genuine message, writing the sentence "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" repeatedly in the narrator's own hand on a single sheet of paper. The aim was to make the partner's death appear a voluntary walk-away, so others would believe the partner had chosen to leave rather than been killed—serving the narrator's own interest and helping deflect suspicion. The fatal flaw was that no real message would repeat the identical sentence over and over; the duplication, in the narrator's own handwriting, was a giveaway. When the note is read aloud, the narrator realizes the repeated copying and the hand will be recognized as theirs, not the partner's. Knowing the fabricated cover-up is about to collapse and expose the killing, the narrator sighs resignedly: "I know I'm in trouble."
